assets.content:
Subject: Turn each blog post into email
Preview text: Keep publishing on your site; let your RSS feed supply the newsletter.

Publish on your site. Send from the feed.

Hi there,

Your blog can remain where the writing begins. With Buttondown, its RSS feed can also supply the email your subscribers receive.

Buttondown is an email newsletter platform with RSS-to-email automation. Build one template around your feed, choose the per-new-item cadence, and a newly published item can trigger an email without a separate round of newsletter composition.

Buttondown checks the feed every thirty minutes, so the trigger follows that interval rather than firing instantly. RSS-to-email is a $9-per-month add-on to the base offering.

The official Buttondown documentation shows how feed fields populate the template and how the per-item cadence works. Review the mechanism, then decide whether it fits the way you publish.

See the RSS workflow → https://docs.buttondown.com/rss-to-email

- Buttondown

asset_metadata.body:
Your blog can remain where the writing begins. With Buttondown, its RSS feed can also supply the email your subscribers receive.

Buttondown is an email newsletter platform with RSS-to-email automation. Build one template around your feed, choose the per-new-item cadence, and a newly published item can trigger an email without a separate round of newsletter composition.

Buttondown checks the feed every thirty minutes, so the trigger follows that interval rather than firing instantly. RSS-to-email is a **$9-per-month add-on** to the base offering.

The official Buttondown documentation shows how feed fields populate the template and how the per-item cadence works. Review the mechanism, then decide whether it fits the way you publish.
asset_metadata.single_idea: Configure one RSS template, and Buttondown can use each newly published feed item to trigger a subscriber email—preserving the reader’s site as the publishing source while removing the need to compose that post again for email.

selected_brief.selection_reason: Automatic RSS-to-email directly addresses this audience’s defining job: continuing to publish on its own site while avoiding a second composition workflow for each post. It is more relevant than Buttondown’s broader API, CLI, integration, or archive capabilities.

value_case.reader_benefit: If the reader wants each blog post to become an email, the same RSS content can be sent to subscribers without composing that post again as a separate newsletter.
value_case.mechanism: The reader builds a template that pulls content from the existing RSS feed, then selects the per-new-item cadence so Buttondown checks the feed and triggers an email when a new item appears.
decision_conditions: The RSS email template must be constructed before the automation can populate emails.
The per-post cadence is based on feed checks every thirty minutes, so it is not instantaneous.
RSS-to-email is listed as a paid add-on at an additional $9 per month rather than part of the free base offering.

claim_conditions: Applies when the blog exposes an RSS feed suitable for the template.
Requires manual construction of the RSS email template.
Per-post triggering follows Buttondown’s thirty-minute feed-checking interval.
RSS-to-email is listed as a $9-per-month add-on.
Building an RSS-to-email template that populates the email with feed content; this is required for all cadences, not just digests (R9).

The automatic pull-and-send mechanism (E5) and its per-post cadence (R2) deliver blog content to email without per-post authoring once a template is built once (R9); documented exceptions are that base-64 encoded images in the feed will not render in most email clients (R12) and non-image enclosures such as podcast audio are skipped (R13), and the automatic feed check runs on a thirty-minute interval with a manual 'Check for updates' override available (R14) rather than instant triggering.

The automatic pull/send mechanism and a documented default non-collection policy address the stated automatic-RSS requirement and the specific tracking complaint, but no evidence in the ledger states that Buttondown's feature set excludes CRM-style functionality.
selected_brief.target_audience: A blogger with an existing site and an RSS feed, finally switching their email send-out off Mailchimp after putting it off for a while
selected_brief.job: Get the reader to inspect Buttondown’s documented RSS-to-email mechanism and decide whether its per-post workflow merits an account-level evaluation.
selected_brief.single_idea: Configure one RSS template, and Buttondown can use each newly published feed item to trigger a subscriber email—preserving the reader’s site as the publishing source while removing the need to compose that post again for email.
selected_brief.felt_need: This audience's stated requirement is narrowly an automatic RSS-to-email feature without extra CRM bloat, and at least one blogger who relied on Mailchimp specifically for pulling an RSS feed into a weekly digest found it tracked recipients even after opting out of tracking.
selected_brief.mechanism: Buttondown requires the reader to build a template that pulls from the existing RSS feed. With the per-new-item cadence selected, it checks the feed every thirty minutes and can trigger an email when a new item is published. The RSS-to-email capability is a $9-per-month add-on.
selected_brief.belief_shift: Before: moving the send-out may sound like adopting another place to write every post. After: the reader sees a documented route that keeps the blog and RSS feed as the content source, with one template to configure and a clear paid-add-on condition.
must_not_say: Do not claim that Buttondown omits CRM-style features or has no product bloat; the evidence does not establish that.
Do not promise zero setup, a default no-code RSS template, or an effortless migration.
Do not call RSS-to-email free; it is listed as a $9-per-month add-on separate from the free base offering.
Do not claim delivery is instantaneous; the documented feed-checking interval is thirty minutes.
Do not claim that every recipient currently uses Mailchimp’s RSS automation or writes every newsletter manually.
Do not promise perfect rendering for every feed, podcast audio support, migration time, subscriber growth, higher engagement, or revenue results.
Do not introduce the API, CLI, integrations, archives, custom domains, GDPR claim, or general feature catalogue; they dilute this email’s single workflow argument.
Do not claim Buttondown is cheaper than the recipient’s current configuration without a like-for-like price comparison.
selected_brief.objection: “Will this actually remove separate per-post email composition, or simply replace it with another setup project?” Answer narrowly: a template must be built once, after which the documented per-item cadence can trigger emails from new feed items; do not characterize the broader migration effort.
selected_brief.tone: Warm, direct, and practical, with quiet confidence and no migration theatrics.
selected_brief.next_step_decision: Decide whether Buttondown’s documented RSS template and per-item cadence are suitable enough to justify creating an account and evaluating the workflow with the reader’s feed.
selected_brief.next_step_value: The official page documents this verified fact: Buttondown's RSS-to-email automation can be configured to trigger per new post as it is published.
selected_brief.next_step_limit: Reading the documentation does not confirm how the reader’s specific feed will render, complete a migration, or establish total cost for their subscriber count and configuration.
selected_brief.subject_strategy: Signal the concrete RSS-to-email workflow change to a product-aware blogger: publish on the existing site, then let the feed supply the email. Avoid generic switching language, unsupported savings claims, and vague promises of simplicity.

report.request: Write exactly one email. Write an acquisition email in English. Give a newsletter operator a specific supported reason to evaluate Buttondown and a clear next step.

reader_verdicts.what_it_sells: Buttondown sells an email newsletter platform that would automatically turn new items from my existing blog RSS feed into subscriber emails, removing the separate newsletter-composition step.
reader_verdicts.relevance_feedback: The premise matches my established situation: I already publish on a site with an RSS feed, currently send the writing through Mailchimp, and am finally moving that send-out elsewhere. The promised RSS-to-email automation addresses the narrow function I need. The email does not establish whether it can reproduce a weekly digest, import my Mailchimp subscribers, or meet my tracking preferences.
assumed_experiences: Profile-supported: I publish writing on my own site and have an existing RSS feed.
Profile-supported: I have been using Mailchimp for the email version and am now acting on a delayed decision to leave it.
Profile-supported: I want automatic RSS-to-email functionality without unnecessary CRM complexity.
Email-only: I want each newly published feed item to trigger its own email on a per-item cadence.

brief.reader:
Selected audience: A blogger with an existing site and an RSS feed, finally switching their email send-out off Mailchimp after putting it off for a while.
Research context describes some members of this market, not this recipient's installed tools or experiences. Follow the campaign request when it scopes the job.
Observed situation (grounded; check applicability): A blogger who already writes on their own site (with an existing RSS feed, in one case running for about twelve years) and who has been sending an email version of that writing out through Mailchimp, now acting on a long-deferred decision to move that send-out off Mailchimp.
brief.reader_segment: A blogger with an existing site and an RSS feed, finally switching their email send-out off Mailchimp after putting it off for a while
brief.promise: Once its required template is configured, Buttondown can turn new items from the blogger’s existing RSS feed into subscriber emails without a separate per-post email-writing workflow.
brief.orientation: Buttondown is an email newsletter platform that, once a template is configured, can automatically pull a blog's RSS feed content into an email send without the writer composing the email separately.
brief.arc: Show one concrete workflow change, disclose the setup and price conditions that qualify it, and invite the reader to inspect the documented mechanism before deciding whether to try it.
brief.sequence_rationale: One email is sufficient because the strongest supported acquisition argument is a single operational consequence: reuse the blog’s RSS output for email delivery. The documentation is the smallest useful first step for an unknown relationship because it shows the required template and cadence before the reader creates an account. The brief does not stage an unsupported migration crisis or assume that the recipient has already attempted the switch.

emails.selection_reason: Automatic RSS-to-email directly addresses this audience’s defining job: continuing to publish on its own site while avoiding a second composition workflow for each post. It is more relevant than Buttondown’s broader API, CLI, integration, or archive capabilities.

value_case.reader_benefit: If the reader wants each blog post to become an email, the same RSS content can be sent to subscribers without composing that post again as a separate newsletter.
value_case.mechanism: The reader builds a template that pulls content from the existing RSS feed, then selects the per-new-item cadence so Buttondown checks the feed and triggers an email when a new item appears.
decision_conditions: The RSS email template must be constructed before the automation can populate emails.
The per-post cadence is based on feed checks every thirty minutes, so it is not instantaneous.
RSS-to-email is listed as a paid add-on at an additional $9 per month rather than part of the free base offering.

claim_conditions: Applies when the blog exposes an RSS feed suitable for the template.
Requires manual construction of the RSS email template.
Per-post triggering follows Buttondown’s thirty-minute feed-checking interval.
RSS-to-email is listed as a $9-per-month add-on.
Building an RSS-to-email template that populates the email with feed content; this is required for all cadences, not just digests (R9).

The automatic pull-and-send mechanism (E5) and its per-post cadence (R2) deliver blog content to email without per-post authoring once a template is built once (R9); documented exceptions are that base-64 encoded images in the feed will not render in most email clients (R12) and non-image enclosures such as podcast audio are skipped (R13), and the automatic feed check runs on a thirty-minute interval with a manual 'Check for updates' override available (R14) rather than instant triggering.

The automatic pull/send mechanism and a documented default non-collection policy address the stated automatic-RSS requirement and the specific tracking complaint, but no evidence in the ledger states that Buttondown's feature set excludes CRM-style functionality.
emails.target_audience: A blogger with an existing site and an RSS feed, finally switching their email send-out off Mailchimp after putting it off for a while
emails.job: Get the reader to inspect Buttondown’s documented RSS-to-email mechanism and decide whether its per-post workflow merits an account-level evaluation.
emails.single_idea: Configure one RSS template, and Buttondown can use each newly published feed item to trigger a subscriber email—preserving the reader’s site as the publishing source while removing the need to compose that post again for email.
emails.felt_need: This audience's stated requirement is narrowly an automatic RSS-to-email feature without extra CRM bloat, and at least one blogger who relied on Mailchimp specifically for pulling an RSS feed into a weekly digest found it tracked recipients even after opting out of tracking.
emails.mechanism: Buttondown requires the reader to build a template that pulls from the existing RSS feed. With the per-new-item cadence selected, it checks the feed every thirty minutes and can trigger an email when a new item is published. The RSS-to-email capability is a $9-per-month add-on.
emails.belief_shift: Before: moving the send-out may sound like adopting another place to write every post. After: the reader sees a documented route that keeps the blog and RSS feed as the content source, with one template to configure and a clear paid-add-on condition.
must_not_say: Do not claim that Buttondown omits CRM-style features or has no product bloat; the evidence does not establish that.
Do not promise zero setup, a default no-code RSS template, or an effortless migration.
Do not call RSS-to-email free; it is listed as a $9-per-month add-on separate from the free base offering.
Do not claim delivery is instantaneous; the documented feed-checking interval is thirty minutes.
Do not claim that every recipient currently uses Mailchimp’s RSS automation or writes every newsletter manually.
Do not promise perfect rendering for every feed, podcast audio support, migration time, subscriber growth, higher engagement, or revenue results.
Do not introduce the API, CLI, integrations, archives, custom domains, GDPR claim, or general feature catalogue; they dilute this email’s single workflow argument.
Do not claim Buttondown is cheaper than the recipient’s current configuration without a like-for-like price comparison.
emails.objection: “Will this actually remove separate per-post email composition, or simply replace it with another setup project?” Answer narrowly: a template must be built once, after which the documented per-item cadence can trigger emails from new feed items; do not characterize the broader migration effort.
emails.tone: Warm, direct, and practical, with quiet confidence and no migration theatrics.
emails.next_step_decision: Decide whether Buttondown’s documented RSS template and per-item cadence are suitable enough to justify creating an account and evaluating the workflow with the reader’s feed.
emails.next_step_value: The official page documents this verified fact: Buttondown's RSS-to-email automation can be configured to trigger per new post as it is published.
emails.next_step_limit: Reading the documentation does not confirm how the reader’s specific feed will render, complete a migration, or establish total cost for their subscriber count and configuration.
emails.subject_strategy: Signal the concrete RSS-to-email workflow change to a product-aware blogger: publish on the existing site, then let the feed supply the email. Avoid generic switching language, unsupported savings claims, and vague promises of simplicity.

brief.voice_notes: Match Buttondown’s plainspoken, lightly wry register. Keep the product and RSS mechanism explicit. Avoid hype, aggressive competitor attacks, and claims that the reader’s current workflow is broken.

reasons: The current product fit is partial or carries unresolved scope limits.
allowed_claims: Buttondown's RSS-to-Email feature took about 30 minutes to set up for one customer, versus the time it took to figure out the equivalent feature in Mailchimp.
Buttondown can take an RSS feed, automatically pull in its content, and send it to subscribers.
A customer who switched their RSS-to-email provider from Mailchimp to Buttondown found Buttondown cheaper, more flexible, and less cluttered.
Buttondown's API is available on all plans, including the free plan.
Buttondown's API is rate-limited to prevent abuse, though the limits are generous enough for most use cases.
Buttondown deliberately does not provide official SDKs, investing instead in its OpenAPI spec so any caller can generate a typed client.
Buttondown does not ship an official MCP server and instead recommends pointing an LLM at its OpenAPI spec to build one tailored to the user's workflow.
Buttondown is GDPR-compliant and does not collect any data about newsletter owners or their subscribers by default.
Buttondown supports over 40 integrations for embedding videos, GIFs, songs, posts, and other content.
Buttondown's CLI lets users script their newsletter from CI/CD pipelines, bulk-manage subscribers, and pull analytics — anything doable in the web app is doable from the command line.
Buttondown's RSS-to-email automation can be configured to trigger per new post as it is published.

The free Buttondown base plan (first 100 subscribers) is described as including only a specific set of features, with RSS-to-email listed separately as an add-on rather than as part of that free base.
Buttondown requires the user to manually construct the email template that pulls in RSS feed content; there is no stated no-code default template.
Buttondown offers a manual override to check an RSS feed immediately, separate from the automatic checking cadence, via a 'Check for updates' button.
unresolved_objections: Does Buttondown's documentation state that it deliberately omits CRM-style features some newsletter platforms bundle in?
recommendation.recommended_next_action: Draft only around the addressed needs and the dossier's scope limits. No companies have been qualified; verify recipient fit before outreach.
recommendation.override_risk: Generating outside the eligible slice risks writing to a structurally similar company whose actual need the product cannot support.

intelligence.selected_audience: A blogger with an existing site and an RSS feed, finally switching their email send-out off Mailchimp after putting it off for a while
partial_caveats_injected: Building an RSS-to-email template that populates the email with feed content; this is required for all cadences, not just digests (R9).

The automatic pull-and-send mechanism (E5) and its per-post cadence (R2) deliver blog content to email without per-post authoring once a template is built once (R9); documented exceptions are that base-64 encoded images in the feed will not render in most email clients (R12) and non-image enclosures such as podcast audio are skipped (R13), and the automatic feed check runs on a thirty-minute interval with a manual 'Check for updates' override available (R14) rather than instant triggering.

The automatic pull/send mechanism and a documented default non-collection policy address the stated automatic-RSS requirement and the specific tracking complaint, but no evidence in the ledger states that Buttondown's feature set excludes CRM-style functionality.
